claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Takamori et al., 2006).

claims.claim: TRPM7 KO neurons displayed a more profound short-term synaptic depression in inhibitory synaptic transmission.
claims.source: With the amplitude of evoked IPSCs normalized to the first response, KO neurons displayed a more profound short-term synaptic depression (Figure 6A–B) and a 56% reduction of the steady-state IPSCs (insert in Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting an important role of TRPM7 in the short-term synaptic depression of inhibitory synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from paired whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: TRPM7 KO neurons showed a 56% reduction of the steady-state IPSCs.
claims.source: With the amplitude of evoked IPSCs normalized to the first response, KO neurons displayed a more profound short-term synaptic depression (Figure 6A–B) and a 56% reduction of the steady-state IPSCs (insert in Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting an important role of TRPM7 in the short-term synaptic depression of inhibitory synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from paired whole-cell recordings shown in the insert in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: TRPM7 plays an important role in the short-term synaptic depression of inhibitory synaptic transmission.
claims.source: With the amplitude of evoked IPSCs normalized to the first response, KO neurons displayed a more profound short-term synaptic depression (Figure 6A–B) and a 56% reduction of the steady-state IPSCs (insert in Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting an important role of TRPM7 in the short-term synaptic depression of inhibitory synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TRPM7 KO neurons show enhanced short-term depression in inhibitory synaptic transmission.

claims.claim: Normalized changes of the iGluSnFR fluorescence during the train revealed an enhanced short-term depression in TRPM7 KO neurons.
claims.source: Similar to that observed in the synaptic plasticity measured with evoked IPSCs (Figure 6A–B), normalized changes of the iGluSnFR fluorescence during the train also revealed an enhanced short-term depression in TRPM7 KO neurons (Figure 6D–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from iGluSnFR imaging shown in Figure 6D-E.

claims.claim: The normalized steady-state iGluSnFR signals at the end of the train was reduced by 36% in TRPM7 KO neurons.
claims.source: The normalized steady-state iGluSnFR signals at the end of the train was reduced by 36% in TRPM7 KO neurons (p < 0.001) (insert in Figure 6E, Figure 6—source data 1), implying a significance of TRPM7 in short-term depression of excitatory synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from iGluSnFR imaging shown in the insert in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: TRPM7 is significant in short-term depression of excitatory synaptic transmission.
claims.source: The normalized steady-state iGluSnFR signals at the end of the train was reduced by 36% in TRPM7 KO neurons (p < 0.001) (insert in Figure 6E, Figure 6—source data 1), implying a significance of TRPM7 in short-term depression of excitatory synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that TRPM7 KO neurons show enhanced short-term depression in excitatory synaptic transmission.

claims.claim: TRPM7 is critical for presynaptic short-term synaptic depression via its regulation in synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
claims.source: Given the well-established significance of synaptic vesicle endocytosis in short-term depression (Henkel and Betz, 1995; Hermosura et al., 2005), our data may suggest that TRPM7 is critical for presynaptic short-term synaptic depression via its regulation in synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations showing enhanced short-term depression in TRPM7 KO neurons and the known role of endocytosis in short-term depression.

claims.claim: VGCCs have been shown to be important for endocytosis.
claims.source: Since VGCCs have been shown to be important for endocytosis (Midorikawa et al., 2014; Perissinotti et al., 2008; Xue et al., 2012), it is implied that Ca2+ for endocytosis at the periactive zone may be derived from diffusion of VGCCs-mediated Ca2+ influxes at active zones.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Midorikawa et al., 2014; Perissinotti et al., 2008; Xue et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Exocytosis can be triggered, without activations of VGCCs, by black widow spider venom, caffeine, or veratridine.
claims.source: On the other hand, exocytosis can be triggered, without activations of VGCCs, by black widow spider venom (Ceccarelli and Hurlbut, 1980; Henkel and Betz, 1995), caffeine (Zefirov et al., 2006), or veratridine (Kuromi and Kidokoro, 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ceccarelli and Hurlbut, 1980; Henkel and Betz, 1995; Zefirov et al., 2006; Kuromi and Kidokoro, 2002).

claims.claim: Extracellular Ca2+ is still necessary for synaptic vesicle endocytosis in paradigms where exocytosis is triggered without VGCCs activation.
claims.source: Interestingly, extracellular Ca2+ is still necessary for synaptic vesicle endocytosis in these paradigms, suggesting distinct Ca2+ channels independent of VGCCs for endocytosis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Ca2+ requirements for endocytosis.

claims.claim: A La3+-sensitive Ca2+ channel is indicated to be required for synaptic vesicle endocytosis in Drosophila.
claims.source: Indeed, a La3+-sensitive Ca2+ channel is indicated to be required for synaptic vesicle endocytosis in Drosophila (Kuromi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kuromi et al., 2004).

claims.claim: It has been proposed that a Ca2+-permeable Flower channel may be necessary for synaptic vesicle endocytosis at the neuromuscular junction in Drosophila.
claims.source: While it has been proposed that a Ca2+-permeable Flower channel may be necessary for synaptic vesicle endocytosis at the neuromuscular junction in Drosophila (Yao et al., 2009), the function of Flower as a Ca2+ influx channel in synaptic vesicle endocytosis of mammalian systems remains questionable, since the role of this Ca2+-permeable protein in synaptic vesicle endocytosis was not confirmed at the calyx of Held (Xue et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yao et al., 2009).

claims.claim: The role of Flower as a Ca2+ influx channel in synaptic vesicle endocytosis was not confirmed at the calyx of Held.
claims.source: While it has been proposed that a Ca2+-permeable Flower channel may be necessary for synaptic vesicle endocytosis at the neuromuscular junction in Drosophila (Yao et al., 2009), the function of Flower as a Ca2+ influx channel in synaptic vesicle endocytosis of mammalian systems remains questionable, since the role of this Ca2+-permeable protein in synaptic vesicle endocytosis was not confirmed at the calyx of Held (Xue et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Xue et al., 2012).

claims.claim: A recent study showed that the protein itself, but not the ion channel property of Flower, is important for synaptic vesicle endocytosis elicited by moderate stimulations in rat hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Additionally, a recent study showed that the protein itself, but not the ion channel property of Flower, is important for synaptic vesicle endocytosis elicited by moderate stimulations in rat hippocampal neurons (Yao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yao et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The time course of Ca2+ influx via Flower protein, in the order of 10–60 min, may be too slow for synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
claims.source: Furthermore, the time course of Ca2+ influx via Flower protein, in the order of 10–60 min (Yao et al., 2009), may be too slow for synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the reported time course of Ca2+ influx via Flower protein.

claims.claim: TRPM7 may regulate local Ca2+ levels in specific presynaptic regions close to the periactive zone, sites for synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
claims.source: Taken together, it is reasonable to consider that TRPM7 may regulate local Ca2+ levels in specific presynaptic regions close to the periactive zone, sites for synaptic vesicle endocytosis (Saheki and De Camilli, 2012), although the global Ca2+ level as we have detected within presynaptic terminals is quickly recovered to the resting level after stimulations.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on experimental observations and known localization of endocytosis.

claims.claim: Extracellular Ca2+ may modulate endocytic kinetics of single synaptic vesicles in neurons.
claims.source: This result is in line with our previous study, which demonstrates an importance of extracellular Ca2+ for the kinetics but not the number of single vesicle endocytosis (Yao et al., 2012). Consistently, extracellular Ca2+ may modulate endocytic kinetics of single synaptic vesicles in neurons, although no analysis was performed on whether Ca2+ affects the number of synaptic vesicles involved (Leitz and Kavalali, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Yao et al., 2012; Leitz and Kavalali, 2011).

claims.claim: The enhanced short-term depression in TRPM7 KO neurons may indicate a potential role of TRPM7 in release site clearance.
claims.source: Since it is postulated that clearance of endocytic components from release sites is an important factor for short-term depression (Hua et al., 2013; Neher, 2010), the enhanced short-term depression we have observed in TRPM7 KO neurons may indicate a potential role of TRPM7 in release site clearance, in addition to synaptic vesicle endocytosis as we have proposed.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on experimental observations and known mechanisms of short-term depression.

claims.claim: The degree of short-term depression can be modulated by exocytic parameters, such as release probability and recruitment of release-ready vesicles.
claims.source: It is also reported that the degree of short-term depression can be modulated by exocytic parameters, such as release probability and recruitment of release-ready vesicles (Neher and Sakaba, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Neher and Sakaba, 2008).

claims.claim: A reduction in presynaptic Ca2+ signals during sustained activity in TRPM7 KO neurons could slow down recruitment of release-ready vesicles, which could also lead to an enhanced short-term depression.
claims.source: While our data showed no difference in the release probability between WT and TRPM7 KO neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), a reduction in presynaptic Ca2+ signals during sustained activity in TRPM7 KO neurons (Figure 5C–D) could slow down recruitment of release-ready vesicles, by reducing activations of vesicle priming and Ca2+ sensors in fusion (Chapman, 2008; Pang and Südhof, 2010), which could also lead to an enhanced short-term depression.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on experimental observations and known mechanisms of vesicle recruitment.

claims.claim: TRPM7's ion channel region may be critical for synaptic vesicle endocytosis while its kinase domain may be important for normal synaptic density in CNS neurons under physiological conditions.
claims.source: As an ion channel fused with a C-terminal alpha-kinase (Nadler et al., 2001), TRPM7's ion channel region may be critical for synaptic vesicle endocytosis (the present study) while its kinase domain may be important for normal synaptic density (Liu et al., 2018) in CNS neurons under physiological conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the present study's findings and a citation to published literature (Liu et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Knockdown or conditional KO of TRPM7 impairs spatial learning.
claims.source: It is reported that TRPM7 may be involved in learning and memory in mouse and rat, as knockdown or conditional KO of TRPM7 impairs spatial learning (Liu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Liu et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The role of TRPM7 in learning and memory could reflect its importance in regulating synaptic density and long-term synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons.
claims.source: The authors indicate that the role of TRPM7 in learning and memory could reflect its importance in regulating synaptic density and long-term synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons (Liu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Liu et al., 2018).

claims.claim: A previous study showing that TRPM7 knockdown does not change evoked synaptic responses is conflicting with the interpretation that TRPM7 regulates synaptic density and LTP.
claims.source: However, this interpretation is conflicting with a previous study showing that TRPM7 knockdown does not change evoked synaptic responses, indicative of no change in synaptic density and LTP (long-term potentiation) (Sun et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sun et al., 2009).

claims.claim: TRPC5 regulates synaptic vesicle endocytosis through a mechanism similar to TRPM7.
claims.source: Interestingly, recent studies suggest that TRPC5, which regulates synaptic vesicle endocytosis through a mechanism (Schwarz et al., 2019) similar to TRPM7 as we have observed in the present study, is critical for both short-term synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons (Schwarz et al., 2019) and learning and memory of animals (Bröker-Lai et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Schwarz et al., 2019).

claims.claim: TRPC5 is critical for both short-term synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons and learning and memory of animals.
claims.source: Interestingly, recent studies suggest that TRPC5, which regulates synaptic vesicle endocytosis through a mechanism (Schwarz et al., 2019) similar to TRPM7 as we have observed in the present study, is critical for both short-term synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons (Schwarz et al., 2019) and learning and memory of animals (Bröker-Lai et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Schwarz et al., 2019; Bröker-Lai et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The role of TRPM7 in short-term synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons may presumably account for its functions in learning and memory of animals.
claims.source: Therefore, the role of TRPM7 in short-term synaptic plasticity in excitatory neurons identified here may presumably account for its functions in learning and memory of animals as reported previously (Liu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the present study's findings and previous reports.

claims.claim: TRPM7 is expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons from single cell transcriptome.
claims.source: Notably, physiological roles of TRPM7 in inhibitory neurons remain largely unknown, although TRPM7 is indeed expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons from single cell transcriptome (Huntley et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Huntley et al., 2020).

claims.claim: TRPM7 is important for short-term synaptic plasticity in inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: Our study identifies that TRPM7 is also important for short-term synaptic plasticity in inhibitory neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the present study showing enhanced short-term depression in inhibitory neurons from TRPM7 KO animals.

claims.claim: The reported roles of TRPM7 in learning and memory could be attributed to its modulations of inhibitory synaptic transmission.
claims.source: Given the increasing significance of inhibitory neuronal circuits in learning and memory (Barron et al., 2017), the reported roles of TRPM7 in learning and memory (Liu et al., 2018) could, alternatively, be attributed to its modulations of inhibitory synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the present study's findings and the known role of inhibitory circuits in learning and memory.

claims.claim: Ca2+ influx via TRPM7 is critical for synaptic vesicle endocytosis and consequently short-term synaptic depression.
claims.source: In summary, our study indicates that Ca2+ influx via TRPM7 is critical for synaptic vesicle endocytosis and consequently short-term synaptic depression, thus implying that TRPM7 may be critical for filtering and gain control of synaptic transmission, as short-term synaptic plasticity is an important factor of synaptic computation (Abbott and Regehr, 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the present study.

claims.claim: TRPM7 may be critical for filtering and gain control of synaptic transmission.
claims.source: In summary, our study indicates that Ca2+ influx via TRPM7 is critical for synaptic vesicle endocytosis and consequently short-term synaptic depression, thus implying that TRPM7 may be critical for filtering and gain control of synaptic transmission, as short-term synaptic plasticity is an important factor of synaptic computation (Abbott and Regehr, 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the present study's findings and the known role of short-term plasticity in synaptic computation.

claims.claim: TRPM7 can be fully inhibited by intracellular Mg2+.
claims.source: During electrophysiological recordings, TRPM7 can be fully inhibited by intracellular Mg2+ (Nadler et al., 2001), which justifies our choice of whole-cell pipette solutions with no Mg2+ for electrophysiological recordings in both chromaffin cells and HEK 293 cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Nadler et al., 2001).

claims.claim: Roles of influx of ions, such as Ca2+, via TRPM7 in neurons have been documented under both physiological and pathological conditions.
claims.source: However, roles of influx of ions, such as Ca2+, via TRPM7 in neurons have been documented under both physiological (Krapivinsky et al., 2006) and pathological (Aarts et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2009) conditions, indicating that additional cytoplasmic signaling molecules, which remains unknown so far, may be able to facilitate TRPM7 to bypass tonic inhibitions by intracellular Mg2+ within intact neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Krapivinsky et al., 2006; Aarts et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2009).

claims.claim: TRPM7 can be blocked by extracellular Mg2+.
claims.source: In addition, TRPM7 can be blocked by extracellular Mg2+ (Nadler et al., 2001), and this Mg2+-dependent TRPM7 blockage may be relieved upon membrane depolarizations (Ramsey et al., 2006), a mechanism similar to postsynaptic NMDA receptors (Hunt and Castillo, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Nadler et al., 2001).

claims.source: In addition, TRPM7 can be blocked by extracellular Mg2+ (Nadler et al., 2001), and this Mg2+-dependent TRPM7 blockage may be relieved upon membrane depolarizations (Ramsey et al., 2006), a mechanism similar to postsynaptic NMDA receptors (Hunt and Castillo, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ramsey et al., 2006; Hunt and Castillo, 2012).

claims.claim: Membrane depolarizations will enhance Ca2+ influx via TRPM7 and thus accelerate synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
claims.source: Therefore, it is likely that membrane depolarizations will enhance Ca2+ influx via TRPM7 and thus accelerate synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the known properties of TRPM7.

claims.claim: Many neurons, such as cortical neurons, frequently generate bursts of action potentials in vivo.
claims.source: Interestingly, many neurons, such as cortical neurons, frequently generate bursts of action potentials in vivo (Baranyi et al., 1993; Gray and McCormick, 1996), and these bursts can occur at a very high frequency, up to 300 Hz, in awake animals as reported (Gray and Viana Di Prisco, 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Baranyi et al., 1993; Gray and McCormick, 1996; Gray and Viana Di Prisco, 1997).

claims.claim: Synaptic vesicle endocytosis becomes a limiting factor for synaptic transmission in neurons during high-frequency action potential firings.
claims.source: Since synaptic vesicle endocytosis becomes a limiting factor for synaptic transmission in neurons during high-frequency action potential firings (Kawasaki et al., 2000), it is likely that neurons may require an up-regulation of synaptic vesicle endocytosis to maintain synaptic transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kawasaki et al., 2000).

claims.claim: Roles of TRPM7 in synaptic vesicle endocytosis will be enhanced during high-frequency firings.
claims.source: Therefore, it is speculated that roles of TRPM7 in synaptic vesicle endocytosis will be enhanced during high-frequency firings, which may couple synaptic vesicle endocytosis to neuronal activities.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the known properties of TRPM7 and neuronal activity patterns.

claims.claim: Recent studies have revealed a tight link between neurodegenerative diseases, particularly Parkinson's disease, and proteins that participate in synaptic vesicle endocytosis, such as auxilin, synaptojanin 1, and endophilin.
claims.source: Recent studies have revealed a tight link between neurodegenerative diseases, particularly Parkinson's disease, and proteins that participate in synaptic vesicle endocytosis, such as auxilin (Song et al., 2017), synaptojanin 1 (Cao et al., 2017), and endophilin (Trempe et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Song et al., 2017; Cao et al., 2017; Trempe et al., 2009).

claims.claim: The consequence on synaptic vesicle endocytosis attributed to TRPM7 dysfunctions could be a potential molecular mechanism for TRPM7-related neurodegenerative diseases, such as Guamanian amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and Parkinson's disease.
claims.source: Our evidence for a role of TRPM7 in synaptic vesicle endocytosis suggests that the consequence on synaptic vesicle endocytosis attributed to TRPM7 dysfunctions could be a potential molecular mechanism for TRPM7-related neurodegenerative diseases, such as Guamanian amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and Parkinson's disease (Hermosura et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the present study's findings and the known link between TRPM7 and neurodegenerative diseases.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on TRPM7 as a ubiquitously expressed TRP channel with an alpha-kinase domain that transports divalent cations and is involved in various physiological and pathological processes including neuronal function and disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C17 are all supported by citations to published literature and represent established background knowledge about TRPM7. These claims appropriately contextualize the current study within existing knowledge of TRPM7 structure, function, and roles in neurons.

results.result: TRPM7 knockout chromaffin cells show significantly increased fission-pore duration during endocytosis without changes in the number of endocytic events, vesicle size, or fission-pore conductance. TRPM7 channels specifically open during endocytosis but not exocytosis, as evidenced by reduced ionic current drift at positive membrane potentials in KO cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C27 are well-supported by cell-attached capacitance recordings and double patch recordings shown in Figure 1. The data demonstrate specific endocytic kinetic defects in TRPM7 KO cells with appropriate controls showing no changes in other endocytic parameters. The inference that TRPM7 opens during endocytosis is supported by the ionic current drift data and biophysical calculations.

results.result: TRPM7 is dispensable for catecholamine release from large dense-core vesicles (LDCVs) in chromaffin cells, as demonstrated by carbon fiber amperometry showing no differences in spike frequency, amplitude, kinetics, quantal size, or foot duration between WT and KO cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by comprehensive amperometry data in Figure 2 showing no differences in multiple exocytosis parameters. Claim C32 appropriately cites consistent findings from prior literature. The conclusion that TRPM7 is dispensable for LDCV exocytosis is well-justified by the data.

results.result: TRPM7 KO neurons exhibit impaired synaptic vesicle endocytosis as evidenced by increased time constants of decay in sypHy and vGlut1-pHluorin fluorescence signals at both room temperature and physiological temperature. This defect is not due to altered vesicle reacidification or changes in expression levels of key endocytic proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are well-supported by live-cell imaging data in Figure 3 using multiple reporters (sypHy and vGlut1-pHluorin) at different temperatures. The controls for reacidification rate and endocytic protein expression levels strengthen the conclusion that the defect is specifically in endocytosis. The inference that TRPM7 is important for synaptic vesicle endocytosis is justified.

results.result: TRPM7 does not affect basal synaptic transmission or release probability in CNS neurons, as shown by unchanged IPSC amplitude, paired-pulse ratio, and vesicular release probability in TRPM7 KO neurons. This contrasts with reported roles in PNS sympathetic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by paired whole-cell recordings and pHluorin experiments in Figure 3 supplements showing no changes in exocytosis parameters. Claim C45 is a reasonable inference from these data. Claim C46 appropriately cites prior literature suggesting different roles in PNS neurons. The conclusion is well-supported.

results.result: The ion channel function of TRPM7, rather than its kinase activity, is critical for synaptic vesicle endocytosis. Wild-type TRPM7 but not a non-conducting mutant (TRPM7LCF) rescues endocytic defects in TRPM7 KO cells, as shown by both fission-pore duration measurements and sypHy imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are well-supported by rescue experiments in Figure 4 showing that TRPM7WT but not TRPM7LCF restores normal endocytic kinetics. The control showing complete suppression of TRPM7LCF currents validates the mutant. Claims C51-C52 appropriately address and dismiss the alternative kinase hypothesis with literature support. The conclusion about ion channel function is well-justified.

results.result: TRPM7 functions in Ca2+-dependent synaptic vesicle endocytosis by serving as a Ca2+ influx pathway. The endocytic defect in TRPM7 KO neurons is absent in zero extracellular Ca2+, and KO neurons show reduced presynaptic Ca2+ signals during stimulation trains without changes in single AP-evoked Ca2+ influx, resting Ca2+ levels, or Ca2+ decay kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C60 are well-supported by sypHy experiments in zero Ca2+ and SyGCaMP6f imaging in Figure 5. The data show that the endocytic defect is Ca2+-dependent and that TRPM7 contributes to Ca2+ accumulation during sustained activity without affecting VGCC function or Ca2+ homeostasis. The inference that TRPM7 serves as a Ca2+ influx pathway for endocytosis is well-justified.

results.result: The manuscript discusses that other TRP family members (TRPM7 in macrophages, TRPC5 in hippocampal neurons) also serve as Ca2+ influx pathways for endocytosis, and speculates that TRP channels may be general Ca2+ channels for synaptic vesicle endocytosis across the nervous system.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 appropriately cite relevant literature. Claim C63 is clearly identified as speculation based on widespread TRP expression. This contextualizes the findings appropriately within the broader literature on TRP channels and endocytosis.

results.result: Ca2+ influx via TRPM7 regulates the kinetics of single endocytic events rather than the number of vesicles involved in endocytosis, suggesting a role in vesicle fission. This is consistent with prior work showing that extracellular Ca2+ modulates endocytic kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 integrate the current findings with prior work. The inference in C65-C66 that TRPM7 regulates kinetics rather than number is well-supported by the data in Figure 1 showing unchanged event numbers but increased duration. Claim C67 appropriately cites supporting literature.

results.result: The manuscript discusses evidence for TRPM7 as a vesicular protein, including its activation by PI(4,5)P2 which is concentrated on the plasma membrane but hydrolyzed during endocytosis, and cites prior studies showing TRPM7 localization to synaptic vesicles. The authors acknowledge conflicting evidence from a proteomics survey that did not detect TRPM7.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C77 appropriately cite and discuss prior literature on TRPM7 localization and PI(4,5)P2 regulation. The authors fairly present both supporting evidence (C71-C74) and conflicting evidence (C75) while noting limitations of the proteomics survey (C76-C77). This provides balanced context for interpreting the vesicular localization of TRPM7.

results.result: TRPM7 KO neurons display enhanced short-term synaptic depression in both inhibitory and excitatory synaptic transmission, with 56% reduction in steady-state IPSCs and 36% reduction in steady-state iGluSnFR signals. This suggests TRPM7 is critical for short-term synaptic depression via regulation of synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 are well-supported by paired whole-cell recordings (Figure 6A-B) and iGluSnFR imaging (Figure 6D-E) showing enhanced depression in both inhibitory and excitatory transmission. Claim C84 is a reasonable inference linking the endocytic defects to the plasticity phenotype, supported by citations to the established role of endocytosis in short-term depression.

results.result: The manuscript discusses the identity of Ca2+ channels for endocytosis, noting that while VGCCs are important, exocytosis can be triggered without VGCCs and still requires extracellular Ca2+ for endocytosis. Prior candidates like Flower channel have limitations, and TRPM7 may regulate local Ca2+ levels at periactive zones.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C92 appropriately cite and discuss prior literature on Ca2+ channels for endocytosis and limitations of previous candidates. Claim C93 is clearly identified as speculative reasoning about local Ca2+ regulation. Claim C94 cites supporting literature. This discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings within the field.

results.result: The manuscript discusses alternative mechanisms that could contribute to enhanced short-term depression in TRPM7 KO neurons, including potential roles in release site clearance and reduced recruitment of release-ready vesicles due to decreased Ca2+ signals during sustained activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are clearly identified as speculative reasoning about alternative mechanisms. While these are plausible hypotheses supported by citations to relevant literature, they are not directly tested in the current study. The speculation is appropriate for the Discussion but does not constitute supported findings.

results.result: The manuscript discusses the physiological roles of TRPM7 in CNS neurons, proposing that the ion channel region is critical for synaptic vesicle endocytosis while the kinase domain is important for synaptic density. The role in short-term synaptic plasticity may account for TRPM7's functions in learning and memory, similar to TRPC5.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C103 appropriately integrate the current findings with prior literature on TRPM7 and TRPC5 in learning and memory. Claim C104 is clearly identified as speculative reasoning linking short-term plasticity to learning and memory. The discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings and proposes testable hypotheses.

results.result: TRPM7 is important for short-term synaptic plasticity in inhibitory neurons, and the reported roles of TRPM7 in learning and memory could be attributed to modulations of inhibitory synaptic transmission given the increasing significance of inhibitory circuits in learning and memory.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 appropriately cites literature on TRPM7 expression. Claim C106 is supported by the experimental data on inhibitory synaptic depression. Claim C107 is clearly identified as speculative reasoning but is a reasonable hypothesis given the data and cited literature on inhibitory circuits in learning and memory.

results.result: The study concludes that Ca2+ influx via TRPM7 is critical for synaptic vesicle endocytosis and consequently short-term synaptic depression, implying that TRPM7 may be critical for filtering and gain control of synaptic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data throughout the manuscript. Claim C109 is a reasonable inference from the findings, supported by citation to the role of short-term plasticity in synaptic computation. This represents the main conclusion of the study.

results.result: The manuscript discusses that TRPM7 can be inhibited by intracellular Mg2+ and blocked by extracellular Mg2+, with blockage relieved by membrane depolarization. This suggests that membrane depolarizations during neuronal activity may enhance Ca2+ influx via TRPM7 and accelerate synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 appropriately cite literature on TRPM7 regulation by Mg2+. Claim C114 is clearly identified as speculative reasoning but is a reasonable hypothesis based on the known properties of TRPM7. This discussion addresses an important consideration about TRPM7 function under physiological conditions.

results.result: The manuscript speculates that roles of TRPM7 in synaptic vesicle endocytosis will be enhanced during high-frequency neuronal firing, which may couple synaptic vesicle endocytosis to neuronal activities, given that neurons frequently generate high-frequency bursts in vivo and endocytosis becomes limiting during high-frequency firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 appropriately cite literature on neuronal firing patterns and the role of endocytosis during high-frequency activity. Claim C117 is clearly identified as speculation but is a reasonable hypothesis that could be tested in future work. This discussion appropriately considers the physiological relevance of the findings.

results.result: The manuscript proposes that consequences on synaptic vesicle endocytosis attributed to TRPM7 dysfunctions could be a potential molecular mechanism for TRPM7-related neurodegenerative diseases such as Guamanian ALS and Parkinson's disease, given the tight link between neurodegenerative diseases and proteins involved in synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 appropriately cites literature linking endocytic proteins to neurodegenerative diseases. Claim C119 is clearly identified as speculative reasoning but is a reasonable hypothesis given the data and the known link between TRPM7 mutations and neurodegenerative diseases. This discussion appropriately considers the translational implications of the findings.
